rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: NVIDIA just reported a hundred and fifteen point eight billion dollars in quarterly revenue. But after Jensen Huang, who sets its direction?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A huge quarter answers the demand question. It does not answer the leadership question.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Quite. A very large engine still requires someone to choose the destination.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge. I'm Alex. That's Jamie and Rufus. Wednesday, November eighteenth, twenty twenty-six. This is The AI Edge. Today: NVIDIA's first earnings report without Jensen Huang, new OpenAI models in your coding tools, and Google's assistant is now doing your errands. We'll answer whether any of this actually changes your day.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. What changed in AI, and what does it mean for your next decision?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The Ledger turns the noise into five focused briefings. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O. That’s LEDGR, with no E between G and R. Find the link in our show notes.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our lead story. NVIDIA reported earnings yesterday, November seventeenth — first report since Jensen Huang left. Interim CEO Colette Kress ran the call. And they beat analyst expectations.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I genuinely did not expect that headline.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The lead was: everything is fine. Markets responded accordingly. But.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: There is always a but.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us on location.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Picture an imagined midtown Manhattan trading desk after yesterday’s earnings release — three screens, cold coffee, someone eating a sandwich while watching a ticker. After the closing bell, NVIDIA reported earnings that cleared analyst targets. Colette Kress ran the call, emphasised continuity, and the market exhaled. Not just NVIDIA — AMD up, Broadcom up.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The whole AI hardware sector moved.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which tells you something about where the anxiety actually was.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The market wasn't pricing in collapse. It was pricing in uncertainty. The earnings removed the uncertainty. So the rally isn't celebrating strong results so much as a collective deep breath. The question everyone had been sitting with was: without Jensen Huang, does this machine keep running? Yesterday's answer was — for now, yes.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: "For now, yes" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, Rufus.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It is. Reuters also noted that investors remain concerned about a potential SEC probe. That hasn't resolved. So you have a company that beat on earnings, steadied its supply-chain partners, and still has a legal overhang nobody can price with any precision.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story. Jamie, you were asking about culture before we went to Rufus. What's your read?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: NVIDIA was Jensen Huang's company in a way that's genuinely unusual even for tech. His tenure, his personal conviction on GPU strategy, the way the company became load-bearing infrastructure for AI — that's not a standard CEO relationship. And now Colette Kress, who was CFO, is the one on the earnings call. That is a very different communication style and a very different signal.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Different good or different bad?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Different appropriate-for-the-moment, maybe. CFOs are built for stability messaging, and stability is exactly what the room needed yesterday. But what NVIDIA has to do next — where it invests, what it builds for the next GPU generation, how it answers AMD and the custom silicon that hyperscalers are quietly developing in-house — those are strategic bets that need a vision, not a steady hand on the quarterly numbers.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the earnings call gave us no evidence of who is making those bets.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. It confirms the company is running. It doesn't tell you where it's running to.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The AMD move is worth unpacking though. If you're a buyer nervous about NVIDIA's supply chain, you start hedging toward AMD — that's rational. But if NVIDIA stabilises, the hedging pressure relieves and that bump could unwind quickly.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Or buyers have been diversifying for eighteen months already and this just made it legible.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Heh. That is the more troubling reading for NVIDIA, yes.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The SEC investigation — Reuters flagged it, but it's still vague. Scope unknown, timeline unknown.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is the honest position. We have strong earnings, a known unknown on the legal side, and an open question on strategic direction. Three different clocks running at three different speeds.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So practically: if you have NVIDIA hardware in your infrastructure or your portfolio, the number to watch isn't the stock price. It's chip supply lead times. Earnings say the company is healthy. Lead times will tell you if the product is still moving.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And if you're an IT buyer who's been stalling a procurement decision — the leadership transition alone probably isn't reason enough to pause. The operational side looks intact.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Keep one eye on the SEC situation. That's the variable nobody can price yet. And whoever they name as permanent CEO will say more about NVIDIA's next chapter than any quarterly call.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I'd actually want to know how the internal engineering teams are feeling about that appointment. Because the people who built the GPU roadmap didn't sign up to work for whoever the board picks next. That's not pessimism — it's just how talent retention works in a founder-led company after the founder leaves.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the question we can't answer from an earnings call.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: No. We can answer whether the machine is running. We cannot answer whether the engineers building the next machine still want to be there.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay. November seventeenth. OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol — both live right now in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API. Astra for demanding reasoning and coding, Sol for everyday coding and agent workflows. So: two models. Is that twice as useful or twice the headache?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: My first instinct was "not again with the naming." But the split actually makes sense to me.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Walk me through it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: If you're writing something complex — multi-step reasoning, tricky architecture — you want the heaviest model available. But if you're automating repetitive tasks or spinning up agents, you don't need that. Sol exists so you're not paying for a sledgehammer to tap a nail.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, you made a face when I said "API."

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us to the global desk.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I was calculating. It's a reflex.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I love that your resting face comes with a spreadsheet.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Only for friends. Strangers get an invoice.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And we appreciate the friends-and-family rate. What did you find?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The split creates a decision point. Every time you build something, you have to ask: Astra problem or Sol problem? That's choosing inference cost — the price per request — every time you make an architectural decision. The overhead isn't zero.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: But that's already the world we live in. GPT-4o, o1, whatever came before. Developers are used to picking the right tool.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: They are. I'm just noting it adds up.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the real question is whether the specialization saves you enough time and money to justify the choosing.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: For coding specifically, I think yes. Picture you're in Codex — OpenAI's coding environment — and your day splits into two buckets: hard architectural problems and boilerplate. The boilerplate is probably seventy percent of your day.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Boilerplate being the repetitive structural code every project needs but isn't the interesting part.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The scaffolding. If Sol handles that reliably, your senior engineers are actually solving problems instead of writing the same setup code for the fourth time this month.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The sleeper in this announcement, to me, is tool calling through the Responses API.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Explain that for people who haven't touched the API.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Tool calling means the model can reach out and use external software — run a search, check a database, trigger another process. The Responses API is OpenAI's newer framework that enables it. What's notable is that tool calling is only available through Responses, not through the older Chat Completions pathway.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So if you want your agent to actually do things, rather than just describe doing things, you need the newer plumbing.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which means any team still on the older integration has to migrate before they get the full capability.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's not nothing for a larger company.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: No. But it's a migration with a clear destination, not a wall.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: OpenAI also shipped updated safety materials with this release — tighter restrictions specifically around higher-risk cybersecurity use.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The timing is interesting. You're releasing your most capable coding models and simultaneously saying: here's where the ceiling is for security research. I find it notable that the documentation arrived with the models rather than a month after.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Reassuring or just paperwork? One thing I keep turning over — Sol is for agent workflows, right? But agents need to call tools. And tool calling requires the Responses API. So if you pick Sol specifically because you want agents, you've already committed to the newer framework. The choice makes the migration.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Oh, that's actually a tighter constraint than it sounds. You don't just choose a model. You choose a whole plumbing stack at the same time.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is either elegant design or a very effective way to move developers off the older pathway.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Maybe both.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Probably both.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: What I haven't seen answered is whether the safety restrictions — the tightened cybersecurity ceiling — apply equally to Astra and Sol, or whether Astra gets a stricter ceiling because it's the more capable model.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: OpenAI's documentation doesn't distinguish between the two on that point, as far as we have it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So a security researcher using Sol for what they'd call routine analysis doesn't know if they're inside the boundary or not.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's a genuinely open question. And the kind of thing where "read the documentation" is correct advice that also isn't fully sufficient yet.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Noted. Test the models, check your API pathway, and apparently also read the fine print on cybersecurity use before your security team touches either one.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Cheerful morning listening.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: We're helpful that way. One thing I'd actually push back on slightly — the split assumes developers can predict which bucket a problem falls into before they start. Some of the most expensive tasks start as boilerplate and turn into architectural problems halfway through.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's a fair constraint. Though you could argue it's also recoverable — you route mid-task to Astra if Sol hits its ceiling. The API lets you switch.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Is that how it works in practice, or is that the ideal?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: We don't have real-world data on that yet. What we have is OpenAI's framing and the architecture. The performance delta between the two on actual developer work — that's the number this community will fill in over the next few weeks.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is why the honest advice is: test on your own work, not someone else's benchmark.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Both models are in ChatGPT Work and Codex now. And if you're on the API, that one pathway question — Responses or Chat Completions — is the detail worth checking before anything else.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Possibly the most load-bearing sentence in this whole story.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I'm going to start saying that about everything. 'Check your plumbing stack.' Very empowering advice.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Alex, if everything is breaking news, when are we supposed to get any work done?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the question The Ledger helps you work through: five focused briefings connecting AI news with the decisions in front of you.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The Ledger. Because reading another headline is a marvellous way to postpone deciding anything. I admire the efficiency of the procrastination.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus has diagnosed the problem. The Ledger link is in our show notes. Back to the story.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our third story. Google announced something yesterday that I think is the most consumer-facing AI shift of the week, and it got a bit buried under the model launches.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Gemini Tasks.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Gemini Tasks. Google says Gemini can now make calls and complete errands on your behalf. Rolling out free to hundreds of millions of people across the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: When I read that, I stopped at "make calls."

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Because?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Because that's the one that feels genuinely different. Chatting with an assistant, drafting an email — those are still me, filtered through a machine. But the AI picking up the phone and talking to someone on my behalf? That's the assistant actually acting in the world.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. It crosses from advisory to autonomous. It's doing something, not suggesting something.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The architecture detail Google included is worth unpacking. These tasks run in what they call a hardware-isolated virtual machine dedicated to the user's account.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Translate that.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A virtual machine is essentially a contained computing environment. Hardware-isolated means it's separated at the hardware level from other users' data and processes. So when Gemini is completing a task for you, it's doing so in a container that can't cross-contaminate with someone else's account. That's a meaningful security choice.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's also a meaningful trust-building choice. Because the barrier for me personally is not whether the AI is capable. It's whether I trust that it's only acting on my behalf and not leaking context somewhere else.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Does hardware isolation actually solve that?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It addresses one specific threat. Data leakage between accounts. It doesn't address the AI misinterpreting your request and doing something you didn't intend.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is my actual fear. Not that it steals my data. That it books the wrong thing with complete confidence.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Picture this. You ask Gemini to call a restaurant and book a table for four on Friday. Straightforward. Except the restaurant has a new phone system, there's an automated confirmation loop, and somewhere in that chain Gemini interprets something wrong and you're confirmed for Saturday at four in the afternoon.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And it was done. That's the thing. You didn't get a draft to review. The action happened.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: This is why the distinction between conversational AI and agentic AI matters so much. Conversation: you stay in the loop. Agentic: the loop runs without you.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Google's framing is that this is a broader personal assistance feature, not a narrow developer tool. That framing matters because it means the users are not developers who've thought carefully about edge cases. It's hundreds of millions of ordinary people.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is a compliment to them in one sense — the technology is accessible enough that it doesn't require technical expertise. But it also means the error surface is enormous.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Google did say advanced features start in the US. So the full capability isn't everywhere at once.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And it's worth being clear: this is a consumer assistant, not a general-purpose open web agent. So it's not roaming the internet on your behalf with unlimited scope. The tasks appear to be bounded — calls, errands, the kinds of things you'd ask a helpful personal assistant to handle.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Though "calls and errands" is still pretty broad. I'd want to know more about the edges. What can it do without asking me first? What requires confirmation?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Google hasn't published those details explicitly in what we have. Which means the best advice is probably: start with low-stakes tasks while you learn where the limits are.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's actually good practical advice in general for any autonomous agent feature. Start with things where a mistake is fixable. Restaurant booking: fixable. Medical appointment modification: probably don't automate that yet.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That said — and I want to hold this honestly — the upside here is real. If this works reliably, the people who benefit most aren't the ones who already have assistants. It's the people who don't have time, who juggle a lot, who'd genuinely save an hour a week by not making calls themselves.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is a large population.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A very large population.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And that connects to a broader question this feature raises: when an AI acts on your behalf, how visible is its reasoning to you afterward? Can you see what it said on that call? Can you replay the conversation?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Those are the questions I'd want answered before I hand it my calendar. And I'd want the answers in plain language, not buried in a settings menu.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's what to watch — not just what it can do, but how much of what it did you can actually see afterward.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The shareable exchange here, honestly, is quite simple. Tell someone: Google's AI can now make phone calls for you on your behalf, and it's free and already rolling out to hundreds of millions of people. Pause. Then ask: does that feel exciting or terrifying? Because their answer will tell you exactly how they think about AI autonomy.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's a genuinely good dinner table test.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: It is. And the practical guidance: Gemini Tasks is free, it's rolling out now in six countries, advanced features start in the US. Try it on something low-stakes this week and notice specifically how much it confirms with you before acting. That behavior — how much it checks in — is the most important thing to understand about how it's actually designed.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, show us the AI transformation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Okay. Quick show of hands. Who has ever booked the wrong plumber because you were juggling three browser tabs, a text thread, and somebody's opinions about which plumber was better?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That is oddly specific.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That is suspiciously specific.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It is universally specific. And it is exactly the household chaos this hypothetical scenario is built around.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right, so what is the scenario?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Google announced a Tasks feature in Gemini, with a rollout beginning in the US and several other countries. What Google describes, and I want to be clear this is their claim, is a mode where you switch from Chat to Task —

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: ask for two local service options with opening hours and source links, and explicitly ask it to stop at comparison before taking any action.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So it gathers and waits?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It proposes and waits. The critical part is that you require approval before it books anything, calls anyone, or spends a penny. Make that explicit.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Who is checking the options once it surfaces them?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: You are. That is not optional. Google's announcement describes the capability; it does not guarantee the information is accurate. You take the source links it provides, verify the quoted hours yourself, and count how many corrections the returned information actually needed.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the AI is the errand runner and the human is the fussy customer.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I did not write it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: No, but you delivered it beautifully.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I feel like Rufus just became the subject of his own case study.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I contain multitudes of unverified appointments.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is precisely the problem Tasks is proposing to help with. Hypothetically.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What is the honest limitation here?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Several. Rollout varies by country and account. Calling capability is unavailable in Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana and Nebraska specifically. The AI can make errors. No set of instructions guarantees safe external actions. This is a proposed workflow, not a tested result — and there is no measured time saving or completed booking being claimed anywhere in this scenario.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the errand runner might hand you a wrong address.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The errand runner might hand you a confident wrong address, which is worse. Checking is not optional.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: First step for someone curious?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Low stakes. Find a comparison that does not matter urgently. Two coffee shops, two library branches, something where a mistake costs you nothing. Switch to Task, make the approval requirement explicit in your prompt, and see what it surfaces before you verify a single detail. The workflow earns trust through that verification step —

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: not around it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the fussy customer was right to be fussy.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The fussy customer was doing the job the whole time. The AI just reduces the number of tabs.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's Jamie's AI transformation.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay. The title question we opened with: can you actually automate your daily coding tasks with the new GPT-6.2 models?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Honest answer: probably some of them, yes. If your daily coding tasks include documentation, test generation, boilerplate scaffolding, and you're running them through Codex or the API — Astra and Sol give you two purpose-fit tools for that work. That's a genuine upgrade from before.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The qualification is real-world versus benchmark. We know OpenAI says Astra is for demanding reasoning and Sol is for everyday coding and agents. We don't yet have independent performance data on actual developer workflows. So the right action is testing, not trusting.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the near-term task for any team building automation is figuring out which side of that migration they're on — because that's what determines whether the new capability is available to them at all.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: On NVIDIA: what changed is that the first post-Huang earnings beat expectations, and the hardware sector responded with a rally. What we still don't know is who makes the next big strategic call, and what the SEC situation resolves to. Neither question was answered yesterday.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Monitor chip lead times. That's the operational signal that will tell you whether the supply chain stability is real or performed.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And on Gemini Tasks: Google just made agent-level AI free and mass-market. That's a significant moment. The practical question isn't capability, it's how much autonomy you're comfortable granting before you've seen it make a mistake.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: We're back tomorrow.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Don't book anything you can't cancel. Today’s question for you: When you delegate a task to an AI, what is your biggest fear?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A quick final note: today’s episode was brought to you by The Ledger—decision-grade AI signal for people who cannot afford to be late.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What changed. Who wins. What you do next. That’s The AI Edge. Follow The AI Edge now. Join us next episode for what changes next.
